issues.item: Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military
issues.explanation: Military-themed conversations are hard to reconcile with a life-threatening illness trauma in a 51-year-old school principal; this trigger implies a combat-related context not represented anywhere else in the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar People: Seeing other people that were involved in the event or that look similar
issues.explanation: Avoiding people involved in the event or who look similar fits interpersonal/assault/accident traumas better than life-threatening illness, where there are typically no 'other people involved' in that sense. It is not well supported by the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Future Orientation: Talking about the future
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'talking about the future' as a trigger is plausible, but 'alcohol smell' is hard to connect unless alcohol was part of treatment context; nothing else in the profile supports that association, making this trigger set clinically incoherent.

'People can't be trusted' is more typical of interpersonal trauma and is poorly anchored to a life-threatening illness trauma in the absence of any treatment-related betrayal, conflict, or mistrust themes elsewhere in the profile.

'Crying' is not a trauma cue but an affective response/behavior, so it is clinically incoherent as a trigger item relative to the other trigger items, which are concrete sensory reminders linked to life-threatening illness (alcohol smell, hospital/antiseptic smell).

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted
issues.explanation: A global mistrust appraisal is a poor fit for the rest of the profile and trauma type. In life-threatening illness, the other items center on altered self and self-reliance, while 'People can't be trusted' implies an interpersonal betrayal/threat theme that is not supported by the memory, trigger, or strategy items and does not align well with the otherwise weak/inactive Threat links.

vignette: John, a 51-year-old widowed school principal from North America, experienced a life-threatening illness several years ago. The memory of his hospitalization still haunts him in unexpected ways. A simple whiff of antiseptic or alcohol can trigger a flood of distressing emotions and thoughts that he struggles to manage. John had come to believe that the person he has become is unrecognizable to himself, and this sense of being different from who he once was has been compounded by the realization that his body is no longer reliable. The traumatic experience left him feeling that he can't rely on himself, which has significantly affected how he navigates daily life. One day last week, John walked past a hospital and suddenly felt overwhelmed by an intense emotional response without any clear image or memory of what happened during his illness. He found it hard to deliberately recall the specific details but was hit with the full force of his emotions. These bodily sensations, such as feeling physically back in that moment when he was critically ill, have made him increasingly anxious about being around medical environments. The emotional intensity and lack of clear images lead John to avoid any potential triggers. He began rehearsing conversations before interacting with anyone, cutting off contact with friends and family, and avoiding hospitals or any medical examinations. This avoidance behavior stems from his deep-seated fear that he might not be able to handle a similar situation again. John's isolation has worsened over time. The thought of encountering the antiseptic smell in a hospital or even a conversation about health can send him spiraling into anxiety. He avoids leaving his home and feels trapped by these fears, further reinforcing his negative beliefs that he cannot trust himself or his body to handle such situations. John's fear that his body is unreliable has led to frequent rehearsals of conversations with medical professionals in which he imagines worst-case scenarios. The difficulty in recalling the specific details of his illness, combined with the intense emotional responses, makes him more anxious and less likely to seek medical help when needed. This avoidance reinforces his negative self-appraisals, making him feel increasingly isolated. The memory difficulties and bodily reenactments have made John more prone to avoidant behaviors and negative appraisals. He finds himself constantly on edge, always anticipating a trigger that could bring back the overwhelming emotions he experienced during his illness. His isolation has also affected his work as a school principal, leading him to delegate tasks he once handled with confidence. John's increasing anxiety has reached a point where he can no longer ignore it. The fear of not being able to rely on himself or his body continues to grow, and the emotional intensity without clear memories haunts him daily. He finally decided to seek help when his isolation became too much to bear and his work began to suffer significantly. What frightens John most is the prospect of losing control again, both mentally and physically. However, he hopes that with professional support, he can regain a sense of reliability in himself and trust his body once more. He seeks therapy not only to manage his symptoms but also to find a way back to being the person he recognizes as himself.
